claim: A large-scale random EMS-mutagenesis screen for mutants that cause increased expression of rpt-3p::gfp isolated 21 alleles affecting proteasome subunit genes.
source: To explore the genetic defects that can activate such proteasome response pathways and the mechanisms that control proteasome subunit gene expression, we performed a large-scale random EMS-mutagenesis screen for mutants that cause increased expression of rpt-3p::gfp. We isolated 21 alleles affecting proteasome subunit genes, including mutations affecting components of the 19S regulatory particle and the 20S catalytic core of the proteasome (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes performing a genetic screen and reports the number and types of alleles isolated, with reference to supporting data in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The isolated proteasome mutant alleles include mutations affecting components of the 19S regulatory particle and the 20S catalytic core of the proteasome.
source: We isolated 21 alleles affecting proteasome subunit genes, including mutations affecting components of the 19S regulatory particle and the 20S catalytic core of the proteasome (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states the types of proteasome components affected, with supporting data shown in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Many of the proteasome mutants show temperature sensitive defects in fertility.
source: Many of the mutants show temperature sensitive defects in fertility, consistent with previous genetic analysis of proteasome function in C. elegans germline development (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) (Shimada et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript reports temperature-sensitive fertility defects with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and cites previous work by Shimada et al., 2006.

claim: Temperature-sensitive fertility defects in proteasome mutants are consistent with previous genetic analysis of proteasome function in C. elegans germline development.
source: Many of the mutants show temperature sensitive defects in fertility, consistent with previous genetic analysis of proteasome function in C. elegans germline development (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) (Shimada et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states consistency with prior work and cites Shimada et al., 2006.

claim: Some proteasome mutant strains show severe temperature sensitive developmental defects that may reflect temperature-sensitivity of the mutant protein.
source: Some proteasome mutant strains show severe temperature sensitive developmental defects that may reflect temperature-sensitivity of the mutant protein (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports temperature-sensitive developmental defects with reference to Table 1 and offers a speculative explanation.

claim: Activation of rpt-3p::gfp in proteasome hypomorphic mutants requires skn-1.
source: Activation of rpt-3p::gfp in proteasome hypomorphic mutants requires skn-1 and depletion of SKN-1 by RNAi causes larval lethality in all but one of the mutant strains, although skn-1(RNAi) is not larval lethal in wild type (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports genetic requirement for skn-1 with supporting data in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Depletion of SKN-1 by RNAi causes larval lethality in all but one of the proteasome mutant strains.
source: Activation of rpt-3p::gfp in proteasome hypomorphic mutants requires skn-1 and depletion of SKN-1 by RNAi causes larval lethality in all but one of the mutant strains, although skn-1(RNAi) is not larval lethal in wild type (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the effect of skn-1 RNAi on proteasome mutants with supporting data in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: skn-1(RNAi) is not larval lethal in wild type.
source: Activation of rpt-3p::gfp in proteasome hypomorphic mutants requires skn-1 and depletion of SKN-1 by RNAi causes larval lethality in all but one of the mutant strains, although skn-1(RNAi) is not larval lethal in wild type (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that skn-1 RNAi does not cause larval lethality in wild type, with reference to Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A wide range of perturbations to proteasome function trigger SKN-1A activation.
source: These data indicate that a wide range of perturbations to proteasome function trigger SKN-1A activation and confirm that compensatory upregulation of proteasome subunit genes by SKN-1A is critical for survival of proteasome dysfunction, either due to mutations or pharmacological inhibition (Keith et al., 2016; Lehrbach and Ruvkun, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the genetic screen data and cites supporting references.

claim: Compensatory upregulation of proteasome subunit genes by SKN-1A is critical for survival of proteasome dysfunction due to mutations or pharmacological inhibition.
source: These data indicate that a wide range of perturbations to proteasome function trigger SKN-1A activation and confirm that compensatory upregulation of proteasome subunit genes by SKN-1A is critical for survival of proteasome dysfunction, either due to mutations or pharmacological inhibition (Keith et al., 2016; Lehrbach and Ruvkun, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion with citations to Keith et al., 2016 and Lehrbach and Ruvkun, 2016.

claim: The genetic screen also identified three alleles of unc-54, which encodes a myosin class II heavy chain (MHC B) expressed in the body wall muscle.
source: Our large genetic screen also identified three alleles of unc-54, which encodes a myosin class II heavy chain (MHC B) expressed in the body wall muscle (Ardizzi and Epstein, 1987; Epstein et al., 1974).
evidence: The manuscript reports the isolation of unc-54 alleles and cites references for the gene identity and expression pattern.

claim: UNC-54 is the major MHC B in body wall muscles.
source: UNC-54 is the major MHC B in body wall muscles and unc-54 loss of function mutations cause paralysis.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this fact about UNC-54.

claim: unc-54 loss of function mutations cause paralysis.
source: UNC-54 is the major MHC B in body wall muscles and unc-54 loss of function mutations cause paralysis.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this phenotype of unc-54 loss of function mutations.

claim: The unc-54 alleles isolated in the screen activate rpt-3p::gfp specifically in body wall muscle cells.
source: The unc-54 alleles we isolated activate rpt-3p::gfp specifically in body wall muscle cells (Figure 1a,b), unlike the proteasome mutations which activate rpt-3p::gfp in many tissues.
evidence: The manuscript reports tissue-specific activation with reference to Figure 1a,b.

claim: Proteasome mutations activate rpt-3p::gfp in many tissues.
source: The unc-54 alleles we isolated activate rpt-3p::gfp specifically in body wall muscle cells (Figure 1a,b), unlike the proteasome mutations which activate rpt-3p::gfp in many tissues.
evidence: The manuscript contrasts the tissue-specificity of unc-54 alleles with proteasome mutations.

claim: The temperature-sensitive unc-54(e1301) and unc-54(e1157) alleles encode mutant forms of UNC-54/MHC B that are prone to misfold and aggregate.
source: The temperature-sensitive unc-54(e1301) and unc-54(e1157) alleles encode mutant forms of UNC-54/MHC B that are prone to misfold and aggregate (Ben-Zvi et al., 2009; Gidalevitz et al., 2006; Silva et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript states this property of the alleles and cites supporting references.

claim: Both unc-54(e1301) and unc-54(e1157) activate expression of rpt-3p::gfp in muscle cells.
source: Both unc-54(e1301) and unc-54(e1157) activate expression of rpt-3p::gfp in muscle cells (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: The manuscript reports activation of the reporter with reference to Figure 1a,b.

claim: unc-54(e190) is a null (deletion) allele that eliminates MHC B expression and causes paralysis regardless of temperature.
source: By contrast, unc-54(e190), a null (deletion) allele that eliminates MHC B expression and causes paralysis regardless of temperature (Dibb et al., 1985), does not activate rpt-3p::gfp (Figure 1a,c,e).
evidence: The manuscript describes the allele properties and cites Dibb et al., 1985.

claim: unc-54(e190) does not activate rpt-3p::gfp.
source: By contrast, unc-54(e190), a null (deletion) allele that eliminates MHC B expression and causes paralysis regardless of temperature (Dibb et al., 1985), does not activate rpt-3p::gfp (Figure 1a,c,e).
evidence: The manuscript reports the lack of reporter activation with reference to Figure 1a,c,e.

claim: All of the unc-54 alleles isolated in the screen are missense mutations that cause temperature-sensitive paralysis similarly to unc-54(e1301).
source: Interestingly, all of the unc-54 alleles we isolated in our screen for proteasome subunit activation are missense mutations that cause temperature-sensitive paralysis similarly to unc-54(e1301) (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the mutation types and phenotypes with reference to Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: rpt-3p::gfp activation is triggered by the presence of mutant forms of MHC B that are prone to misfold, not simply by loss of MHC B or defective muscle function.
source: These data suggest that rpt-3p::gfp activation is triggered by the presence of mutant forms of MHC B that are prone to misfold, not simply by loss of MHC B or defective muscle function.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation based on the comparison of different unc-54 alleles.

claim: Activation of rpt-3p::gfp expression by temperature-sensitive mutant MHC B is completely lost in skn-1a(mg570) mutant animals that lack SKN-1A but retain other SKN-1 isoforms.
source: Activation of rpt-3p::gfp expression by temperature-sensitive mutant MHC B is completely lost in skn-1a(mg570) mutant animals that lack SKN-1A but retain other SKN-1 isoforms (Figure 1d,e).
evidence: The manuscript reports the genetic requirement for SKN-1A with reference to Figure 1d,e.

claim: Increased levels of SKN-1A[∆DBD]::GFP accumulate specifically in the body wall muscle cells of unc-54(e1301) and unc-54(mg519) animals but not in the wild type.
source: We found increased levels of SKN-1A[∆DBD]::GFP accumulates specifically in the body wall muscle cells of unc-54(e1301) and unc-54(mg519) animals but not in the wild type (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports protein accumulation data with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Expression of temperature-sensitive mutant UNC-54/MHC B triggers rpt-3p::gfp expression via activation of SKN-1A.
source: We conclude that expression of temperature-sensitive mutant UNC-54/MHC B triggers rpt-3p::gfp expression via activation of SKN-1A.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the genetic and reporter data.

claim: Transgenic C. elegans that express human Aβ in muscle cells show adult-onset defects in muscle function.
source: Transgenic C. elegans that express human Aβ in muscle cells (unc-54p::Aβ) show adult-onset defects in muscle function and serve as a model for the cell biology of Aβ accumulation and toxicity (Link, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript states this property of the transgenic model and cites Link, 2006.

claim: Transgenic C. elegans expressing human Aβ in muscle cells serve as a model for the cell biology of Aβ accumulation and toxicity.
source: Transgenic C. elegans that express human Aβ in muscle cells (unc-54p::Aβ) show adult-onset defects in muscle function and serve as a model for the cell biology of Aβ accumulation and toxicity (Link, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript states this use of the model and cites Link, 2006.

claim: Aβ expression in muscle triggers strong muscle-specific activation of rpt-3p::gfp.
source: We found that Aβ expression in muscle triggers strong muscle-specific activation of rpt-3p::gfp, which is lost in skn-1a(mg570) mutant animals that lack the transmembrane-domain-containing Nrf1 orthologue SKN-1A (Figure 1f).
evidence: The manuscript reports reporter activation with reference to Figure 1f.

claim: Aβ-induced activation of rpt-3p::gfp is lost in skn-1a(mg570) mutant animals that lack the transmembrane-domain-containing Nrf1 orthologue SKN-1A.
source: We found that Aβ expression in muscle triggers strong muscle-specific activation of rpt-3p::gfp, which is lost in skn-1a(mg570) mutant animals that lack the transmembrane-domain-containing Nrf1 orthologue SKN-1A (Figure 1f).
evidence: The manuscript reports the genetic requirement for SKN-1A with reference to Figure 1f.

claim: hsf-1(sy441) is a hypomorphic allele that disrupts chaperone regulation.
source: hsf-1 encodes the C. elegans orthologue of HSF1, which regulates expression of multiple cytoplasmic chaperones under proteotoxic stress conditions such as elevated temperature (Fujimoto and Nakai, 2010). hsf-1(sy441) is a hypomorphic allele that disrupts chaperone regulation (Hajdu-Cronin et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript describes the allele and cites Hajdu-Cronin et al., 2004.

claim: hsf-1(sy441) mutant animals develop normally at lower temperatures, but arrest larval development at 25°C.
source: hsf-1(sy441) mutant animals develop normally at lower temperatures, but arrest larval development at 25°C, presumably due to the toxic accumulation of misfolded proteins in the cytoplasm.
evidence: The manuscript reports the temperature-dependent phenotype.

claim: Larval arrest of hsf-1(sy441) at 25°C is presumably due to the toxic accumulation of misfolded proteins in the cytoplasm.
source: hsf-1(sy441) mutant animals develop normally at lower temperatures, but arrest larval development at 25°C, presumably due to the toxic accumulation of misfolded proteins in the cytoplasm.
evidence: The manuscript offers a speculative explanation for the phenotype.

claim: hsf-1(sy441) L4 larvae raised at 20°C show unaltered expression of rpt-3p::gfp compared to the wild type.
source: hsf-1(sy441) L4 larvae raised at 20°C show unaltered expression of rpt-3p::gfp compared to the wild type.
evidence: The manuscript reports reporter expression data.

claim: rpt-3p::gfp expression is significantly increased in hsf-1 mutant animals following upshift to 25°C for 24 hr.
source: However, rpt-3p::gfp expression is significantly increased in hsf-1 mutant animals following upshift to 25°C for 24 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports reporter expression data with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Activation of rpt-3p::gfp in the hsf-1 mutant requires SKN-1A.
source: This activation of rpt-3p::gfp in the hsf-1 mutant requires SKN-1A (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports the genetic requirement with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: SKN-1A is broadly activated under conditions that increase the cellular burden of unfolded proteins.
source: These results indicate that SKN-1A is broadly activated under conditions that increase the cellular burden of unfolded proteins.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the hsf-1 mutant data.

claim: There are likely many endogenous proteins that, when misfolded, are able to trigger a SKN-1A-dependent response.
source: It is therefore likely that there are many endogenous proteins that, when misfolded, are able to trigger a SKN-1A-dependent response.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this inference.

claim: The SKN-1A response is sensitive enough to detect a single - albeit abundant - unfolded protein.
source: The effects of the unc-54ts mutants and unc-54p::Aβ indicate that this response is sensitive enough to detect a single - albeit abundant - unfolded protein.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the unc-54 and Aβ data.

claim: At least in muscle, the SKN-1A response is cell autonomously elicited by protein misfolding, but not by mutations that severely compromise muscle function without misfolded protein expression.
source: Further, at least in muscle, the response is cell autonomously elicited by protein misfolding, but not by mutations - such as the unc-54(e190) deletion - that severely compromise muscle function without misfolded protein expression.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on comparison of different unc-54 alleles.

claim: The proteasomal response does not depend on cellular or organismal consequences of tissue dysfunction in general.
source: This proteasomal response therefore does not depend on cellular or organismal consequences of tissue dysfunction in general.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion.

claim: SKN-1A is activated as part of a cell-autonomous response to cytoplasmic unfolded proteins.
source: Taken together these data strongly suggest that SKN-1A is activated as part of a cell-autonomous response to cytoplasmic unfolded proteins.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the collective data.

claim: The peptide:N-glycanase PNG-1/NGLY1, the aspartic protease DDI-1/DDI2 and the ERAD component SEL-1/SEL1 are each necessary to activate SKN-1A in response to direct proteasomal insults.
source: The peptide:N-glycanase PNG-1/NGLY1, the aspartic protease DDI-1/DDI2 and the ERAD component SEL-1/SEL1 are each necessary to activate SKN-1A in response to direct proteasomal insults (Lehrbach and Ruvkun, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript states this requirement and cites Lehrbach and Ruvkun, 2016.

claim: The SKN-1A-dependent rpt-3p::gfp transcriptional response to Aβ is lost in png-1(ok1654) and ddi-1(mg571) mutants.
source: The SKN-1A-dependent rpt-3p::gfp transcriptional response to Aβ is lost in png-1(ok1654) and ddi-1(mg571) mutants and is diminished in sel-1(mg457) mutants (Figure 1g).
evidence: The manuscript reports the genetic requirements with reference to Figure 1g.

claim: The SKN-1A-dependent rpt-3p::gfp transcriptional response to Aβ is diminished in sel-1(mg457) mutants.
source: The SKN-1A-dependent rpt-3p::gfp transcriptional response to Aβ is lost in png-1(ok1654) and ddi-1(mg571) mutants and is diminished in sel-1(mg457) mutants (Figure 1g).
evidence: The manuscript reports the genetic requirement with reference to Figure 1g.

claim: Related, or possibly identical, mechanisms govern SKN-1A activation by both direct assaults on the proteasome and the presence of misfolded and/or aggregated proteins.
source: We conclude that related, or possibly identical, mechanisms govern SKN-1A activation by both direct assaults on the proteasome and the presence of misfolded and/or aggregated proteins.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the genetic pathway analysis.

claim: Over-expression of an active site mutant of the β5 subunit of the 20S proteasome in otherwise wild-type cells causes proteasome dysfunction in yeast and the mouse.
source: Over-expression of an active site mutant of the β5 subunit of the 20S proteasome in otherwise wild-type cells causes proteasome dysfunction in yeast and the mouse (Heinemeyer et al., 1997; Li et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript states this fact and cites Heinemeyer et al., 1997 and Li et al., 2004.

claim: The myo-3p::pbs-5[T65A] transgene causes muscle-specific activation of the rpt-3p::gfp proteasome subunit reporter.
source: The myo-3p::pbs-5[T65A] transgene causes muscle-specific activation of the rpt-3p::gfp proteasome subunit reporter in a manner closely resembling that caused by mutant MHC B and Aβ (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: The manuscript reports reporter activation with reference to Figure 2a,b.

claim: Activation of rpt-3p::gfp by myo-3p::pbs-5[T65A] is lost in skn-1a(mg570) mutants.
source: This activation is lost in skn-1a(mg570) mutants, consistent with a SKN-1A-dependent response to proteasome dysfunction (Figure 2a).
evidence: The manuscript reports the genetic requirement with reference to Figure 2a.

claim: Wild type animals carrying the myo-3p::pbs-5[T65A] transgene show mildly impaired locomotion compared to non-transgenic controls.
source: Wild type animals carrying the myo-3p::pbs-5[T65A] transgene show mildly impaired locomotion compared to non-transgenic controls (Figure 2c).
evidence: The manuscript reports locomotion data with reference to Figure 2c.

claim: The locomotor rate of wild type animals carrying the myo-3p::pbs-5[T65A] transgene is reduced to a similar extent in day 1 and day 7 adults showing that this mild defect is not exacerbated by age.
source: The locomotor rate of wild type animals carrying the myo-3p::pbs-5[T65A] transgene is reduced to a similar extent in day 1 and day 7 adults showing that this mild defect is not exacerbated by age (Figure 2c).
evidence: The manuscript reports age-dependent locomotion data with reference to Figure 2c.

claim: Wild-type muscle cells are robust to proteasomal insults and are able to maintain near-normal function despite the presence of the mutant β5 subunit.
source: This suggests that wild-type muscle cells are robust to proteasomal insults and so are able to maintain near-normal function despite the presence of the mutant β5 subunit.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation of the locomotion data.

claim: The myo-3p::pbs-5[T65A] transgene causes complete paralysis in skn-1a(mg570) mutant animals lacking the SKN-1A-mediated proteasomal response pathway.
source: By contrast, the myo-3p::pbs-5[T65A] transgene causes complete paralysis in skn-1a(mg570) mutant animals lacking the SKN-1A-mediated proteasomal response pathway (Figure 2d).
evidence: The manuscript reports the phenotype with reference to Figure 2d.

claim: SKN-1A mediates cell-autonomous activation of proteasome subunit genes in response to proteasome impairment.
source: We conclude that SKN-1A mediates cell-autonomous activation of proteasome subunit genes in response to proteasome impairment, and that this SKN-1A-dependent compensation is essential for maintaining function in muscle cells experiencing proteasome dysfunction.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the myo-3p::pbs-5[T65A] data.

claim: SKN-1A-dependent compensation is essential for maintaining function in muscle cells experiencing proteasome dysfunction.
source: We conclude that SKN-1A mediates cell-autonomous activation of proteasome subunit genes in response to proteasome impairment, and that this SKN-1A-dependent compensation is essential for maintaining function in muscle cells experiencing proteasome dysfunction.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the paralysis phenotype in skn-1a mutants.

claim: Aggregation-prone proteins including human Aβ may interact with proteasomes and impair their function.
source: Aggregation-prone proteins including human Aβ may interact with proteasomes and impair their function (Ayyadevara et al., 2015; Deriziotis et al., 2011; Gregori et al., 1995; Kristiansen et al., 2007; Snyder et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript states this possibility and cites multiple supporting references.

claim: The UB(G76V)::GFP ubiquitin fusion protein is normally degraded by the proteasome, but accumulates to detectable levels if proteasome function is impaired.
source: The UB(G76V)::GFP ubiquitin fusion protein is normally degraded by the proteasome, but accumulates to detectable levels if proteasome function is impaired (Johnson et al., 1995; Segref et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript describes the reporter and cites Johnson et al., 1995 and Segref et al., 2014.

claim: The rpl-28p::ub(G76V)::gfp reporter reveals a muscle-specific proteasomal defect in myo-3p::pbs-5[T65A] transgenic animals.
source: As expected, this reporter of proteasome activity reveals a muscle-specific proteasomal defect in myo-3p::pbs-5[T65A] transgenic animals (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the reporter data with reference to Figure 3a,b.

claim: Stabilization of UB(G76V)::GFP in PBS-5[T65A]-expressing muscle cells is greatly enhanced in the skn-1a mutant.
source: Stabilization of UB(G76V)::GFP in PBS-5[T65A]-expressing muscle cells is greatly enhanced in the skn-1a mutant – all mutant animals show accumulation of GFP in all muscle cells and at higher levels than the wild type (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the reporter data with reference to Figure 3a,b.

claim: The SKN-1A transcriptional program partially corrects the muscle proteasomal defect caused by the myo-3p::pbs-5[T65A] insult.
source: These data show that the SKN-1A transcriptional program partially corrects the muscle proteasomal defect caused by the myo-3p::pbs-5[T65A] insult.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the UB(G76V)::GFP data.

claim: The severe locomotor defects and paralysis of myo-3p::pbs-5[T65A] animals that lack SKN-1A likely stem from enhanced defects in proteasome function.
source: The severe locomotor defects and paralysis of myo-3p::pbs-5[T65A] animals that lack SKN-1A therefore likely stem from enhanced defects in proteasome function.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: unc-54p::Aβ does not stabilize UB(G76V)::GFP in wild type animals.
source: However, in contrast to myo-3p::pbs-5[T65A], we did not observe stabilization of UB(G76V)::GFP in unc-54p::Aβ transgenics (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the lack of reporter stabilization with reference to Figure 3a,b.

claim: unc-54p::Aβ only weakly affects UB(G76V)::GFP levels within the muscle cells of skn-1a mutants: about 10% of skn-1a(mg570) Aβ-expressing animals show weak accumulation of UB(G76V)::GFP in some muscle cells suggesting a mild impairment of proteasome function.
source: unc-54p::Aβ only weakly affected UB(G76V)::GFP levels within the muscle cells of skn-1a mutants: about 10% of skn-1a(mg570) Aβ-expressing animals showed weak accumulation of UB(G76V)::GFP in some muscle cells suggesting a mild impairment of proteasome function (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the reporter data with reference to Figure 3a,b.

claim: unc-54(e1301) and unc-54(mg519) have no effect on UB(G76V)::GFP degradation in the muscle in the skn-1a(mg570) mutant background.
source: We also tested the effect of unc-54(e1301) and unc-54(mg519) in the skn-1a(mg570) mutant background and found no effect on UB(G76V)::GFP degradation in the muscle (Figure 3b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the reporter data with reference to Figure 3b.

claim: In mammalian cells, UbG76V::GFP accumulates only in cells with severely compromised proteasome function, as measured by Suc-LLVY-AMC hydrolysis in cell lysates.
source: In mammalian cells, UbG76V::GFP accumulates only in cells with severely compromised proteasome function, as measured by Suc-LLVY-AMC hydrolysis in cell lysates (Dantuma et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript states this property of the reporter and cites Dantuma et al., 2000.

claim: Very low concentrations of bortezomib (2 ng/ml) cause increased accumulation of UB(G76V)::GFP in skn-1a mutant animals.
source: We found that very low concentrations of bortezomib (2 ng/ml) cause increased accumulation of UB(G76V)::GFP in skn-1a mutant animals.
evidence: The manuscript reports the bortezomib dose-response data.

claim: Wild type animals exposed to 2 ng/ml bortezomib do not show activation of rpt-3p::gfp.
source: But wild type animals exposed to bortezomib at the same concentration do not show activation of rpt-3p::gfp.
evidence: The manuscript reports the bortezomib dose-response data.

claim: Monitoring UB(G76V)::GFP accumulation in a skn-1a mutant background serves as a more sensitive indicator of proteasome impairment than rpt-3p::gfp expression in wild type animals.
source: This suggests that monitoring UB(G76V)::GFP accumulation in a skn-1a mutant background serves as a more sensitive indicator of proteasome impairment than rpt-3p::gfp expression in wild type animals.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation of the bortezomib data.

claim: The UB(G76V)::GFP reporter should be sensitive enough to detect impairment of proteasome function, if this were the mechanism through which misfolded MHC B or Aβ cause activation of rpt-3p::gfp.
source: As such, the UB(G76V)::GFP reporter should be sensitive enough to detect impairment of proteasome function, if this were the mechanism through which misfolded MHC B or Aβ cause activation of rpt-3p::gfp.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this reasoning.

claim: SKN-1A may be activated by misfolded proteins even in the absence of impaired proteasome function.
source: These results therefore suggest that SKN-1A may be activated by misfolded proteins even in the absence of impaired proteasome function.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the UB(G76V)::GFP data.

claim: There is no difference in locomotion rate between the wild type and skn-1a(mg570) mutants during the first week of adulthood.
source: We found no difference in locomotion rate between the wild type and skn-1a(mg570) mutants during the first week of adulthood (Figure 4a).
evidence: The manuscript reports locomotion data with reference to Figure 4a.

claim: The locomotion of animals harboring unc-54(e1301) or unc-54(mg519) mutations is strongly modulated by age in a SKN-1A-dependent manner.
source: In contrast to wild type, the locomotion of animals harboring unc-54(e1301) or unc-54(mg519) mutations is strongly modulated by age in a SKN-1A-dependent manner (Figure 4b,c).
evidence: The manuscript reports age-dependent locomotion data with reference to Figure 4b,c.

claim: The unc-54ts mutants show a severe locomotion defect on day 1 of adulthood, but recover to near-normal rates of locomotion on days 3–7.
source: The unc-54ts mutants show a severe locomotion defect on day 1 of adulthood, but remarkably, recover to near-normal rates of locomotion on days 3–7.
evidence: The manuscript reports the age-dependent locomotion pattern.

claim: During aging the capacity for correct folding and function of mutant MHC B improves.
source: This suggests that during aging the capacity for correct folding and function of mutant MHC B improves.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation of the locomotion recovery.

claim: Age-dependent changes in proteostasis and physiology may include activation of protective responses that improve protein folding or function.
source: Although age-dependent changes in proteostasis and physiology are thought to be largely detrimental, this suggests that in some cases they may include activation of protective responses that improve protein folding or function.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation.

claim: The beneficial effect of age on unc-54ts locomotion is entirely dependent on SKN-1A.
source: Strikingly, this beneficial effect of age is entirely dependent on SKN-1A.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the double mutant data.

claim: unc-54(mg519); skn-1a(mg570) double mutants show no age-dependent improvement in locomotion.
source: unc-54(mg519); skn-1a(mg570) double mutants show no age-dependent improvement in locomotion and unc-54(e1301); skn-1a(mg570) double mutants show a slight age-dependent decline in locomotion (Figure 4b,c).
evidence: The manuscript reports locomotion data with reference to Figure 4b,c.

claim: unc-54(e1301); skn-1a(mg570) double mutants show a slight age-dependent decline in locomotion.
source: unc-54(mg519); skn-1a(mg570) double mutants show no age-dependent improvement in locomotion and unc-54(e1301); skn-1a(mg570) double mutants show a slight age-dependent decline in locomotion (Figure 4b,c).
evidence: The manuscript reports locomotion data with reference to Figure 4b,c.

claim: The age-dependent genetic interaction between unc-54ts and skn-1a is not allele-specific, but rather a general effect of SKN-1A on the function of misfolding MHC B.
